content: Urinary dipsticks are occasionally utilized for screening individuals who do not exhibit any symptoms, as well as for identifying potential cases among hospitalized or outpatient individuals without genitourinary complaints. Abnormal findings detected during such screenings may prompt further diagnostic evaluations, which could uncover significant conditions such as bladder cancer or chronic kidney disease (CKD). While early detection through urinary dipstick screening has the potential to improve patient outcomes, it also carries the risk of leading to unnecessary follow-up procedures, some of which may be invasive, and unwarranted treatments. The objective of this review was to evaluate and quantify both the potential benefits and harms associated with the use of urinary dipsticks for screening purposes in general populations and hospitalized patients. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted within the Cochrane Renal Group's Specialised Register up to September 8, 2014. The search strategy involved collaboration with the Trials Search Coordinator and employed terms relevant to the topic under investigation. The inclusion criteria for this review specified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and other study designs that compared urinary dipstick screening with no screening. The review sought studies that examined the detection of various markers, including haemoglobin, protein, albumin, albumin-creatinine ratio, leukocytes, nitrite, or glucose, either individually or in combination, across any clinical setting. Studies involving patients with pre-existing urinary disorders were excluded from consideration. The data collection and analysis plan involved two independent authors extracting data from the included studies and assessing the risk of bias using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. However, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. The literature search identified 4298 records, of which 4249 were excluded based on title and abstract screening. Of the remaining 49 records (representing 44 studies) that underwent full-text assessment, 18 studies were excluded because they were not RCTs, and 26 studies were excluded because they compared interventions or controls that were irrelevant to the review's objectives. Consequently, no studies were deemed eligible for inclusion. In conclusion, this review found no evidence to determine the benefits or harms of urinary dipstick screening. As a result, the effectiveness and potential risks associated with this screening method remain unknown.
